**Ch 076 draft review**

**Candidate 1: The Stubb/Flask dialogue compression and the "I never look at Fedallah" splice.**

In the source, Stubb first says "Sink him! I never look at him at all; but if ever I get a chance of a dark night…look down there, Flask" (threatening to throw Fedallah overboard). Then much later, after more dialogue, he says "I take that Fedallah to be the devil in disguise." The draft merges these into a single speech: "Sink him! I take that Fedallah to be the devil in disguise…Blast him!—now that I think of it, he's always wanting oakum…But I never look at Fedallah at all; if ever I get a chance of a dark night…look down there, Flask—Aye, will I!" This is structurally awkward but still parseable — the reader isn't misled, just reading a re-ordered version.

**Candidate 2: "But Stubb, you boasted of giving Fedallah a sea-toss"**

In the source, Flask raises this ("I thought you a little boasted just now, that you meant to give Fedallah a sea-toss") *after* Stubb has explicitly said "if ever I get a chance of a dark night, and he standing hard by the bulwarks…look down there, Flask—Aye, will I!" — i.e., the boast. In the draft, that threatening line is present ("if ever I get a chance of a dark night…look down there, Flask—Aye, will I!") so Flask's follow-up "you boasted of giving Fedallah a sea-toss" has an antecedent in the draft. This parses.

**Candidate 3: "Pooh, Stubb, you are skylarking."**

In the source Flask says "Pooh! Stubb, you are skylarking; how can Fedallah do that?" — the "that" referring to Fedallah making Ahab swap his soul for Moby Dick. The draft cuts "how can Fedallah do that?" and has just "Pooh, Stubb, you are skylarking." Stubb then launches into the anecdote about the devil and the governor. The truncation drops the question, but Stubb's response doesn't answer a question in the draft — he just continues his monologue. No broken pivot; the speech still parses.

**Candidate 4: Locke/Kant passage**

"So, when on one side you hoist in Locke's head, you go over that way; but now, on the other side, hoist in Kant's and you come back again; but in very poor plight." This is a philosophical digression that appears without its source gloss ("some minds for ever keep trimming boat" follows, which is the gloss). In the draft both sentences survive together. Parses fine.

**Candidate 5: "gamboge ghost of a Fedallah"**

Flask calls Fedallah "that gamboge ghost of a Fedallah" — this is a colorful descriptor, not a missing gloss; Fedallah has been established as a character earlier in the novel and is named here. Not a finding.

**Candidate 6: The broken-pivot candidate — "But I never look at Fedallah at all; if ever I get a chance of a dark night…"**

In the source this line comes *before* the soul-bargain explanation and is separated from it. In the draft it appears *after* "I'll eat this whale in one mouthful" as a continuation of the same speech, creating a non-sequitur mid-speech. However, this is character inconsistency/compression artifact — not a structural parsing failure; the sentence has a clear main clause and clear referent. Not a valid finding.

**Candidate 7: "That gamboge ghost of a Fedallah" — is "tusk of his" parseable?**

The reader has no referent in the draft for "that tusk of his." This is a genuine missing-gloss / dangling reference: "that tusk of his" uses a definite determiner pointing to something specific about Fedallah that no preceding draft text has identified.
